5153.dq: Since tone (like stress) is a feature of the word and all combinations of L H and D are found, compressions of tones are common in one-syllable words.
5153.prule: No positional stress rule. Ekajuk is a two-level tone language (H, L, plus automatic downstep D). Stress is called lexical and 'goes normally with the high tones', i.e. it is a correlate of high tone rather than an independent position computable from syllable count or weight. A closed set of morphemes (object-pronoun clitics -m -a -e -r -n, the clitic -a, and the initial vowel of area 'much', eji 'when', ana 'like that', owo 'then') carries inherent stress whatever its tone.
5153.quote: [ms p. 7, sec. 1.4.2 f) Stress and Tone] Stress and tone are both lexical. Stress goes normally with the high tones. (see phon.) tn.quote: There are two tonal levels in Ekajuk, namely high (H) and low (L) plus a feature of downstep lowering automatically all high tones after low tones within certain grammatical units. After a downstep a new pitch level is established, although the interval between H and L is gradually narrowed. The symbol D is used for an established downstepped high tone. Since tone (like stress) is a feature of the word and all com- binations of L H and D are found, compressions of tones are common in one-syllable words. Compressed tones are written with juxtapposed letterss. HL for downglide, LH for upglide.

5155.dloc: SIL 77207 typed, p. 2 (items 1-40); SIL 77200 typed, p. 2 (items 1-40) and handwritten original, p. 3 (items 41-88); SIL 77208 handwritten original, pp. 2-3 (items 1-88) and typed copy, p. 2
5155.prule: No rule is stated in any reachable source: the three SIL items are bare Expanded Philippine Word List field sheets whose only key is '? = glottal'. Nickell writes an acute on one vowel of most entries, on the ultima in some words (abaká, kagát, uták, toláng, isú?, sikə́d, maluwág, natáy, aggáw, masiddúg, ilibúng) and on the penult in others of the same shape (mapúray, sínay, gáta?, dúpa, dígu?, dága?, sámi, útta, lárəm, masíddug), so the marks are not computable from syllable count; but the acute is nowhere defined, the same words are marked on different syllables in the two lists made two days apart in neighbouring villages (77207 masiddúg, gáta?, butalí?, daga?, gatang vs 77200 masíddug, gatə́?, butáli?, dága?, gátang), forms marked in one copy are unmarked in another (dakəl, ngamin, sinay, dulay), and in the only Faire-proper list by another hand (77208 original) every penult acute sits on a colon-marked long vowel (dá:ga, á:tu?, amí:mum, talí:nga?) while uncoloned words take the acute on the ultima (anák, algáw, dabbúm). The 77208 pattern is what the Whittle & Lusted 1963 Pamplona analysis (primary stress on the ultima; long vowels with secondary stress and a pitch rise that sounds like primary stress) predicts a fieldworker would write, and Nickell's uncoloned penult acutes may be long vowels he did not mark (he colons only gí:dam and ma:sú in items 1-40). The sheets are therefore consistent both with lexically placed penult/ultima stress and with fixed ultima stress plus contrastive length, and cannot decide between them.
5155.srule: Not mentioned in Nickell 1981 (SIL 77207 Calassitan, Faire; SIL 77200 Annip, Rizal) or SIL 77208 (Bullakit, Faire), all pages read: 1966 Expanded Philippine Word List field sheets with one undefined acute per word and no prose; only key '? = glottal'.

5159.dq: Das Ur-Ambon betonte alle mehr als einsilbigen Wörter auf der Pänultima des Grundwortes. Einsilbige Suffixe, welcher Art auch, übten auf die Lage des Tones keinen Einfluß aus.

5159.prule: Stress on the penultimate syllable of the base word (Grundwort); monosyllabic suffixes did not move it (the Ur-Ambon/Sub-Ambon rule, p.174, restated p.110 § 124). 5163.tone: Meinhof 1916-17: 217-219: Katla has 'musikalische Töne' 'neben dem dynamischen Akzent'; he first believed a dynamic (stress) accent was present, later concluded that musical tones exist alongside it, and admits 'Den Hochton habe ich, wie es leicht geschieht, besonders zuerst oft, als Stärkeakzent aufgefaßt' (p. 218), i.e. many of his stress percepts were the high tone. Katla data on p. 218 are marked with high and low tones (Hochton, Tiefton), with the same word often noted with different tones by the two informants B. and S.; tones appear 'sogar auf stimmhaften Konsonanten'; Klingenheben ('Klg.') also noted pitch and recorded tone changes in context (gu 'Hund' changes tone between high tones; mumwin 'Elefant' after a high tone). tn.quote: Bei dem Versuch, das Katla zu schreiben, glaubte ich erst, daß ein dynamischer Akzent vorläge. Eine Reihe von Notizen sind deshalb mit ′ d. h. mit Stärkeakzent versehen. Später überzeugte ich mich, daß neben dem dynamischen Akzent musikalische Töne vorliegen wie in andern Sudansprachen. ... Den Hochton habe ich, wie es leicht geschieht, besonders zuerst oft, als Stärkeakzent aufgefaßt. ... Es kam nur darauf an, das Vorhandensein der musikalischen Töne nachzuweisen, und das ist, so viel ich sehe, gelungen. Nähere Untersuchung über ihre Gesetze muß der Einzelforschung überlassen bleiben.
tn.translation: When attempting to write Katla I at first believed that a dynamic (stress) accent was present. A number of notes are therefore marked with ′, i.e. with stress accent. Later I convinced myself that alongside the dynamic accent musical tones are present, as in other Sudan languages. ... The high tone I have often, as easily happens, especially at first, taken for stress accent. ... The point was only to demonstrate the presence of the musical tones, and that, as far as I can see, has succeeded. Closer investigation of their laws must be left to specialised research.

5165.prule: None: no word-stress rule. Kɔnni is a tone language (two basic tone levels, High and Low, plus a downstepped High after a High, sec. 6.1.1 p. 338; tone is lexically and grammatically contrastive). Cahill examines stress explicitly (sec. 6.7) and finds no phonetic correlate (vowel length, amplitude) that is significant and independent of tone: in two words with the same LH tone sequence on the first two syllables, greater amplitude falls on the second syllable in kùléhé 'the tortoises' but on the first in kùlí 'tortoise'. Conclusion: stress is not phonologically contrastive or distinctive, and (p. 39) 'stress plays no part in the phonology of Konni'. No stress position is given.
5165.srule: None: the source denies word stress altogether, so there is no secondary stress to place ('it appears that stress is not phonologically contrastive or distinctive in Konni', p. 466; 'stress plays no part in the phonology of Konni', p. 39). 5165.tone: Two basic tone levels, High and Low, with a downstepped High after a High (sec. 6.1.1, p. 338; minimal and near-minimal tone pairs listed there); downstep treated as the phonetic result of a floating Low; floating High as the associative morpheme; tonal polarity (chapter 6 overview, p. 39). On stress the source says there is no phonetic correlate (vowel length, amplitude) significant and independent of tone, amplitude does not fall consistently on one syllable, and 'stress plays no part in the phonology of Konni' (p. 39). Cahill also notes that other Gur descriptions (Dagaare penultimate stress per Antilla & Bodomo 1996; Supyire and Buli root/word-initial 'stressed' syllables or greater 'articulatory energy' per Carlson 1994 and Kroger 1992) may be describing word-initial position rather than stress; those remarks concern other languages, not Kɔnni.

5167.dq: primary stress is assigned to the main verb if it is not part of the major presupposition of the sentence, and to the head of the focus NP if the main verb is presupposed.
5167.dloc: p. 29, section 3 'Phonological rules', A 'Pre-cycle rules', (a) 'Stress assignment'; tone statement p. 22, section 'Non-consonants'.
5167.prule: Sentence-level, syntax-assigned: primary stress falls on the main verb unless the verb is part of the major presupposition of the sentence, in which case it falls on the head of the focus NP (examples 1-2: the same string 'Asa is here' is stressed on 'here' as an answer to 'Where is Asa?' and on 'is' as an answer to 'What is Asa doing?'). No word-level position rule is stated.
5167.srule: Sentence-level, assigned by the syntax like the primary: secondary stress on the first syllable of the head noun of each component NP and of the head verb when these have not received primary stress; tertiary stress on syntactic markers (for a bisyllabic marker the stressed syllable is specified by the syntactic component). No word-internal rhythmic/alternating stress is described.
5167.quote: The assignment of primary stress is difficult to state without a detailed explanation of the syntactic component of Lisu grammar. Surface strings from that component are assigned linear order by topicalisation and focus rules (see Hope 1972) and primary stress is assigned to the main verb if it is not part of the major presupposition of the sentence, and to the head of the focus NP if the main verb is presupposed. ... 5170.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Chapter I 'Pronunciation' has sections on vowel length (1.3), nasalisation (1.6), tone (1.7, cross-referenced to Ch. V) and syllable patterns (1.8) but no stress or accent section. 5177.dq: Word stress is also assigned from right to left. Both vowels and syllable final consonants following a single vowel contribute to syllable weight. Length in vocoids is most accentuated when the word occurs at the end of a phonological phrase. [p. 6; word stress is named as such and phrase-final position is invoked only for vowel length]

5177.heavy: Both vowels and syllable final consonants following a single vowel contribute to syllable weight. [p. 6] -- i.e. a long vowel or vowel sequence (VV, VVC) and a short vowel plus coda consonant (VC) are heavy/bimoraic; a consonant after a long vowel does not add weight ('a final consonant or syllable following a long vowel' is extrametrical).
5177.dflt: penult: two light syllables form one right-aligned trochee (['mɑ̞ko] /mɑ.ko/ 'no, not', [ɑ̞nu̞'nu̞zi̞] /ɑ.nu.nu.zi/ 'their souls', ['ɑ̞mɑ̞] /ɑ.mɑ/ 'Daddy', [t̪ i̞ 'lɑ̞lɑ̞] /ti-lɑ.lɑ/ '3PL habitually go' with the prefix skipped); a lone CV word is a degenerate stressed foot (te 'ocean', li 'poison', lu 'armband', mbi 'Trochus', pa, to)
5177.prule: Stress is predictable and quantity-sensitive: bimoraic (moraic) trochees are built from right to left over the word, with long vowels/vowel sequences and a coda consonant after a short vowel making a syllable heavy. Primary stress falls on the rightmost foot, so in the transcribed examples the final syllable is stressed when heavy ([i̞ 'rɑ̞:β] /i-rɑɑβ/ 'go sailing', [i̞ 'sɛŋ] /i-sɛŋ/ 'knock', [nɑ'u̞m] /nɑ.um/ '1SG-steal', [ɑ̞i't̪ ɑ̞r] /ɑi.tɑr/ 'large wooden spoon', [mɑ̞'lɑ̞u̞] /mɑ.lɑu/ 'for a long time', [t̪ ɑ̞mɑ̞'mɑ̞i̞] /tɑmɑmɑi/ '1PL exclusive father', [ɑ̞ŋɑ̞'ŋɑ̞o] /ɑ.ŋɑ.ŋɑo/ 'spider'); a long-vowel syllable is stressed and the consonant or syllable after it is extrametrical ([ɑ̞ri̞ 'ɑ̞:ŋ] /ɑ.ri.ɑɑŋ/, [i̞ pɑ̞du'du:ŋ] /i-pɑduduuŋ/ 'correct, teach', [t̪ i̞ n't̪ i̞:nɑ̞] /tintiinɑ/ 'big ones', ['ɑ̞:t̪ ɛ] /ɑɑtɛ/ 'his liver'); otherwise the penult is stressed (['mɑ̞ko] /mɑ.ko/ 'no, not', [ɑ̞nu̞'nu̞zi̞] /ɑ.nu.nu.zi/ 'their souls', ['ɑ̞mɑ̞] /ɑ.mɑ/ 'Daddy'). Never stressed (extrametrical): a final consonant or syllable after a long vowel, the subject-indexing prefixes ([t̪ i̞ 'lɑ̞] /ti-lɑ/ '3PL-go', [u̞'lɑ̞] /u-lɑ/ '2SG-go'), word-final transitive suffixes, and the plural prefix -xa on inalienable nouns. Monosyllabic CV words form degenerate one-syllable feet and are stressed. Stress is manifested by increased amplitude, length and pitch; vowel length is contrastive independently of stress (p. 8 minimal pairs). The surface statement 'final if heavy, else penult' is my reading of the metrical description plus the transcribed examples; the source itself states the rule only in foot terms.
5177.srule: Stated only for morphology: the transitivity-altering verb prefixes pa 'causative', va (T) ~ wa (O) 'reciprocal', par 'reciprocal' and ma 'detransitivizing' 'seem to be inherently stressed, since they always receives secondary stress, regardless of the canonical shape of the verb root' (p. 7). Rhythmic secondary stresses on non-final feet are implied by the right-to-left bimoraic trochaic footing (p. 6) but are not stated as such, and no transcribed example (pp. 2-9, words up to five syllables) carries a secondary-stress mark, so their placement is not given.

5178.prule: Right-edge, vowel-length-sensitive: words of three or more syllables are stressed on the antepenult unless the antepenult is short and the penult long, in which case the penult; disyllables are stressed on the penult, but on the ultima when both vowels are short. tn.quote: 2a. Tone. Tone is both lexical and grammatical. In the MORU-MA'DI languages so far investigated (MORU, MA'DI, LOGO, LUGBARA) and in LENDU, three tone levels have been established, and the same would seem to be the case with MANGBUTU-EFE. According to Larochette, however, there are only two tonemes in MANGBETU-MEJEI.¹ Falling and Rising tones are found only in MANGBETU-MEJE, where they occur in long syllables which are virtually disyllabic. In all languages there are Tone Classes in Nouns and Verbs.
tn.cite: Tucker, Archibald N. & Margaret A. Bryan. 1966. Linguistic Analyses: The Non-Bantu Languages of North-Eastern Africa (Handbook of African Languages). London: Oxford University Press for the International African Institute (repr. Routledge 2017).
tn.locator: Ch. 1 'The Moru-Mangbetu languages', sec. 2 'Tone and Stress', 2a 'Tone', 1966 p. 30 (= Routledge 2017 reprint PT37)
tn.note: Three tone levels, tone both lexical and grammatical, with tone classes in nouns and verbs; no falling or rising tones reported for Lendu; the levels are not named and Lendu stress is not described.
